results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

results.quote: This glossary defines the book's terms and links each to the chapter explaining its use, including [[commerce-data-and-analytics]] and [[inventory-and-availability]].
results.finding: The intro-only reader predicted one definition per term with an owning-chapter link, the confusable pairs, sections by part plus an alphabetical index and the dated-source material, but could not predict the opening reading-conventions section (evidence labels, take-away tiers, growth stages, failure patterns), the separate standards-and-regulations and fictional-names tables, the slash rows, or that Kestrel & Pine is fictional; the expected answer requires all of these. The introduction's last sentence repeats its first instead of naming them (the reader flagged the repetition and the unexplained choice of the two linked chapters). Note: spec roadmap.placement puts part of the roadmap in the How to Use section, which AC-4 excludes; the cheapest fix is in the draft (replace the repeated sentence with the page's parts), so fault is draft.

All 20 outliner summaries match the controlling idea of their aligned spec paragraph (p01-p20). Minor drift only: the Preface unit lists 'evidence labels, conditional recommendations and failure patterns' where p05 names take-away tiers and scale stages (reported under flow_is_followable). Scope: the page is ~17,000-19,000 words, over the 8,000-word threshold, so the full-page reverse-outline and flow readings were NOT run; the outliner saw the prose units only; this result covers only the sample the readers saw (introduction, the prose units, the first six rows of each table and the first three index letters), not the ~390 rows.

results.quote: A storefront's 'order' can differ from an invoice or warehouse shipment.
results.finding: The outliner read two ideas: what the page offers, and examples of terms that cause errors. Spec p01 makes the examples the reason for the page ('because terms like order and in stock mean different things'); the draft states the purpose, gives the examples without tying them to it, then restates the purpose, so the examples read as a separate idea. Lead with the examples as the reason and state the purpose once.

How to Use ¶3 was marked two_ideas (Kestrel & Pine is fictional; legal/standards/vendor rows are summaries). Spec p04's controlling idea joins both as the limits of how far a row can be trusted, and the paragraph matches it; judged one idea. All other units single-idea. Scope: the page is ~17,000-19,000 words, over the 8,000-word threshold, so the full-page reverse-outline and flow readings were NOT run; covers only the sample the readers saw (introduction, the prose units, the first six rows of each table and the first three index letters), not the ~390 rows.

Every prose unit traces to a supporting claim: intro, How to Use ¶1 and the index to G1; How to Use ¶2, the eleven part intros and the conclusion to G2; How to Use ¶3 and Standards to G3; How to Use ¶3 and Kestrel to G4. Judged on the prose units (the readers' sample); individual table rows were not judged.

Each of the 15 tables is introduced by its section paragraph, which says what the rows define and names the owning chapters (Standards also explains its scope and date columns). The index is a list, not evidence. Judged on the section paragraphs and the first six rows of each table only.

How to Use (elaboration: 'Browse by the book's parts or jump to the alphabetical index' picks up the opening's lookup), p03 (elaboration: 'The 392 rows give short teaching definitions'), p04 (additional_support: fictional names and summary-only legal rows) and the sequence boundaries into the Preface, Parts I-XI, Standards and Kestrel (each paragraph opens on the next group of terms) express the declared relationships. Parts V, VII, VIII, X and XI open with verbless fragments rather than the declared sentence form; the heading carries the sequence, so not failed here (see flow_is_followable).
